NeuroGraph ANGPBIOLOGY

Biological analogy

From neural tissue to distributed consensus

ANGP borrows its organizational principles from the most successful distributed system known to science — the human brain. This is an architectural analogy, not biological equivalence. The protocol does not simulate neurons; it adopts the same five-stage pipeline that biological neural systems use to turn local perception into coherent global cognition.

The five-stage mapping

Each biological principle becomes a protocol primitive

The diagram above is not metaphorical decoration. Every box on the right side of the figure is a real, implemented component of the ANGP protocol — and every box on the left is the well-established neuroscience principle it was derived from. The mapping is one-to-one and complete.

Stage 01

Local perception

Each neuron in the brain observes only its immediate chemical and electrical environment — it has no global view of the entire brain, no awareness of distant cortical regions, and no access to a centralized map of activity. Perception is built from the bottom up, one synapse at a time.

Local ledger view

Each ANGP node maintains only a local shard of the ledger and communicates with a small set of peers. No single node ever holds the complete global state, yet coherent consensus emerges from the aggregate of these limited local views — exactly as cognition emerges from limited neurons.

Stage 02

Continuous signaling

Neurons do not fire binary on/off pulses in the way computers process bits. They encode information in graded analog signals — firing rates, dendritic potentials, and neurotransmitter concentrations that vary continuously across a spectrum. This richness allows fine-grained, parallel, and noise-tolerant communication.

Prediction vector

ANGP nodes emit continuous prediction vectors — high-dimensional numerical arrays describing what they believe the next global state should be. Unlike traditional blockchains that exchange discrete vote messages, ANGP nodes exchange continuous signals that can be aggregated statistically rather than counted.

Stage 03

Hebbian adaptation

The principle articulated by Donald Hebb in 1949 — “neurons that fire together, wire together” — describes how synaptic strength increases between co-active cells. This local, unsupervised learning rule is now understood to underlie memory formation, skill acquisition, and adaptive cortical remapping throughout life.

Hebbian learning

ANGP nodes adapt their internal prediction models using the same principle: when a node’s prediction aligns with the emerging consensus, that prediction pathway is reinforced. When it diverges, the model self-corrects. Learning is local, continuous, and unsupervised — no global coordinator tells nodes how to update.

Stage 04

Population coding

Meaning in the brain is not stored in any single neuron. It is distributed across populations of neurons that fire together in characteristic patterns. Sensory perception, motor commands, and abstract thought all emerge from the collective activity of thousands or millions of neurons acting in concert.

Weighted median

ANGP aggregates the prediction vectors of all participating nodes using a weighted median — a robust statistical estimator that resists outliers and Byzantine manipulation far better than simple majority voting. The median requires no leader, no rounds, and no quorum threshold; it converges as a property of the population itself.

Stage 05

Emergent cognition

No region of the brain “knows” the whole picture. There is no homunculus, no central executive, no seat of consciousness issuing commands. Coherent perception arises as an emergent property of billions of neurons interacting through local rules — one of the deepest and most counterintuitive findings of modern neuroscience.

Emergent consensus

ANGP consensus is similarly emergent. There is no leader, no committee, no validator set with special privileges, and no voting round in which nodes explicitly agree. The global state crystallizes from the collective prediction activity of all nodes — a self-organizing property that makes the protocol leaderless, roundless, and resistant to capture.

Why this matters

Consensus without leaders, votes, or rounds

Traditional distributed consensus — whether Paxos, Raft, Practical Byzantine Fault Tolerance, or proof-of-stake voting — relies on the same fundamental scaffold: a leader proposes, validators vote, and a quorum threshold decides. This scaffold introduces well-known failure modes: leader capture, validator cartel formation, long-range attacks, and the structural centralization that emerges when only a small set of nodes can realistically participate in quorum.

ANGP removes the scaffold entirely. There is no leader because there is no proposal step — every node continuously emits its own prediction vector. There is no vote because predictions are aggregated by a statistical median, not counted as discrete ballots. There is no round because consensus is a continuous emergent property of the network, not a discrete event. The biological analogy is not aesthetic — it is the reason the protocol can sustain 200,000 transactions per second under a 90% adversary without ever needing to elect, vote, or finalize a block in the traditional sense.

Scope of the analogy. The mapping presented here is architectural, not biological. ANGP does not simulate spiking neurons, model dendritic computation, or attempt to reproduce the biochemical complexity of living neural tissue. The analogy refers strictly to organizational principles — local observation, continuous signaling, local learning rules, population-level aggregation, and emergent global coherence — that biological neural systems and the ANGP protocol both employ to solve the same problem: producing coherent global state from many limited local participants.

NeuroGraph ANGPARCHITECTURE

Layered protocol design

A six-layer architecture for emergent decentralized consensus

ANGP combines DAG transaction ordering, VRF proposer selection, reputation-weighted median consensus, dual-EMA reputation scoring, asynchronous attack detection, and gossip-based P2P synchronization. Unlike classical blockchains that rely on sequential blocks and proof-of-work, ANGP organizes transactions in a DAG, selects proposers via cryptographic lottery, and achieves consensus through the statistical aggregation of continuous-valued predictions rather than binary voting.

Section 1

Introduction

Decentralized consensus protocols must balance three competing demands: security (resistance to adversarial behavior), scalability (throughput as nodes increase), and decentralization (no central point of control). Classical blockchain protocols like Bitcoin prioritize security and decentralization at the cost of scalability (7 TPS). BFT protocols like Tendermint prioritize security and scalability but sacrifice decentralization (limited to a few hundred validators).

ANGP is designed from the ground up to address all three demands simultaneously. Its architecture is organized into six layers, each with a clear separation of concerns: Network, Data, Sortition, Consensus, Reputation, and Synchronization. Data flows upward (from network to synchronization), while control flows downward — reputation affects sortition and consensus at every step.

Section 2

Network Layer

2.1 Architecture

The network layer provides the communication foundation. It uses TCP-based persistent connections with asynchronous I/O (Tokio runtime) for non-blocking message transmission. Each node maintains:

  • A TCP listener on port 7001 for incoming connections
  • Outbound connections to known peers (from a peer list)
  • A connection pool mapping peer addresses to message channels

2.3 Gossip Protocol

When a node receives a message (transaction, proposal, or finalized batch), it processes it locally and re-broadcasts to all connected peers. This viral propagation reaches the entire network within a few hops (typically 1-2 seconds for 10,000 nodes).

The protocol uses a serialize-once, send-to-all pattern: the message is serialized to bytes once, then the same bytes are sent to all peers, eliminating redundant serialization.

◎
Node A
Read + Write
→
TCP stream
←
◎
Node B
Read + Write

A single TCP stream carries messages in both directions. Node A reads B's messages and writes its own on the same connection — eliminating the need for B to also establish a separate outbound connection to A.

Figure 2. Bidirectional TCP connection. One stream carries messages in both directions, halving connection overhead versus traditional dual-connection patterns.

2.4 Message Types

Three message types are propagated via gossip:

⇅

A new transaction from a user or peer

⚙

↻

L2

Section 3

Data Layer

3.1 DAG Structure

ANGP does not use sequential blocks. Transactions are organized in a directed acyclic graph (DAG). Each transaction references one or more parent transactions ("tips"), creating a graph structure that allows parallel processing.

The genesis transaction (G) is the root. Each subsequent transaction references 2-3 parent tips. When a transaction is finalized, it is no longer a tip; new transactions reference the remaining tips.

3.2 Mempool

The mempool stores pending (unfinalized) transactions. It provides:

  • Add — insert with signature verification
  • Get — retrieve by hash
  • Remove — delete finalized
  • Drain — extract all pending for batch finalization

3.3 Ledger

The ledger stores finalized transactions in a HashMap indexed by hash. It also maintains:

  • last_finalized_nonce — per-sender nonce tracking (replay prevention)
  • batch_index — batch ID to transaction list
  • dag_edges — parent-child relationships for DAG traversal

3.4 State Manager

The state manager tracks account balances:

state = {(address, balance) | address ∈ Accounts}

It supports apply_tx (debit sender, credit receiver), mint (genesis credit), and apply_reward (proposer fee distribution).

Figure 3. DAG transaction structure. Each transaction references 2-3 parent tips. Green nodes are unconfirmed tips (no children yet). When a transaction is finalized it ceases to be a tip; new transactions reference the remaining tips, extending the graph.
L3

Section 4

Sortition Layer

4.1 Cryptographic Node Lottery

At each 200ms step, approximately 1% of nodes are selected as proposers via a Verifiable Random Function (VRF). The selection is:

  • Unpredictable — no one can predict who will be selected
  • Verifiable — anyone can verify that a selection was legitimate
  • Rotating — the committee changes completely at every step

Each node i computes its VRF for step t:

VRFi(t) = Signski("propose_step_" ∥ t ∥ "_shard_" ∥ si)

If the output falls below a reputation-adjusted threshold θi, the node is selected. Because t changes every step, the output is completely different each time, producing a fresh, independent committee.

4.2 Reputation-Adjusted Threshold

The threshold scales with reputation:

θi = θbase · (floor + (cap − floor) · repi)
θ_base
0.01
base selection rate
floor
0.20
minimum weight
cap
1.50
maximum weight

Higher-reputation nodes are selected more frequently; lower-reputation nodes are selected less frequently, creating a natural meritocracy.

θi vs repi

Higher rep → higher θ → more frequent selection

L4

Section 5

Consensus Layer

5.1 Emergent Consensus Model

ANGP replaces binary voting with continuous prediction aggregation. Each node produces a 4-dimensional prediction vector si ∈ ℝ⁴. The consensus is the reputation-weighted median:

cd = WeightedMedian {(s_{i,d}, rep_i) | i ∈ active}

The median is chosen over the mean because it is robust to outliers: a single Byzantine prediction with an extreme value cannot shift the median, whereas it would shift the mean significantly.

5.2 Transaction Approval

Transactions are approved by an observation threshold, not a vote. A transaction is approved if it appears in at least 70% of active proposals:

approved(tx) ⇔ |{p ∈ active : tx ∈ p.seen_txs}| / |active| ≥ 0.70

Nodes do not judge whether a transaction is "good" or "bad" — they simply report which transactions they have seen. Validity is verified independently at mempool insertion.

Section 6

Reputation Layer

6.1 Dual-EMA Scoring

Each node's reputation is tracked by two exponential moving averages:

repfast(i, t) = αf · cert(ei) + (1 − αf) · repfast(i, t−1)
repslow(i, t) = αs · cert(ei) + (1 − αs) · repslow(i, t−1)
α_f = 0.3
fast
reacts in ~3 steps
α_s = 0.1
slow
reacts in ~10 steps

The combined reputation is the arithmetic mean of both.

6.3 Attack Detection

Five specialized detectors run asynchronously in a "slow lane" to identify subtle attack patterns without blocking consensus:

⚠
Clone Detector — Sybil identity cloning
⚠
Coordination Detector — colluding communication patterns
⚠
Adaptive Detector — reputation-aware adaptive behavior
⚠
Temporal Detector — timing-based attacks
⚠
Jump Detector — sudden value discontinuities

Detected nodes receive a reputation penalty of up to 15% per step, compounding over consecutive detections.

6.2 Reputation Zones

Reputation directly affects three aspects of participation:

  • VRF threshold — lower rep → lower threshold → less frequent selection
  • Consensus weight — lower rep → less weight in the median
  • Filtering — below 0.9 → excluded from consensus; below 0.2 → evicted

6.4 Recovery

Nodes with rep ≥ 0.9 that are not proposers in the current step recover toward 1.0 at rate:

β = 0.001 per step

This ensures honest nodes with transient issues recover quickly, while attackers cannot exploit recovery to reset their reputation.

Evicted — effectively silenced. Cannot propose, cannot weigh on consensus, cannot recover without rejoining as a fresh identity.

L6

Section 7

Synchronization Layer

7.1 Cross-Node Sync

After a node finalizes a batch locally, it broadcasts a FinalizedBatchMessage to all peers. This message contains:

  • The sender's identity
  • The step number
  • The full list of finalized transactions
  • The reward map (proposer to fee)

When a peer receives this message, it applies the batch via apply_finalized_batch(): deduplicates, applies state transitions, replicates reward distribution, and inserts transactions into the local DAG ledger.

7.2 Consistency Guarantee

This mechanism ensures ledger consistency across all nodes. Even if a node missed some proposals (due to network latency), it catches up by applying finalized batches from peers. Because all honest nodes receive the same proposals (via gossip) and apply the same consensus rules, they produce the same finalized batches.

Section 9

Design Principles

The ANGP architecture is guided by four design principles that distinguish it from classical blockchain and BFT protocols.

Emergent over imposed

Consensus is not imposed by a leader or a quorum vote. It emerges from the statistical aggregation of independent predictions. No single node decides the outcome; the median is a collective property.

Statistical over deterministic

The protocol relies on statistical properties (median robustness, EMA smoothing, probabilistic detection) rather than deterministic thresholds. This provides natural tolerance to noise, outliers, and partial failures.

Asynchronous over synchronous

The slow-lane attack detection, gossip propagation, and cross-node sync are all asynchronous. Consensus throughput (Layer 4) is never blocked by secondary concerns (Layer 5, Layer 6).

Layered over monolithic

Each layer has a clear responsibility and interface. The network layer does not know about consensus; the consensus layer does not know about attack detection. This separation enables independent optimization and testing.

Section 10

Conclusion

ANGP's six-layer architecture provides a complete framework for decentralized consensus. The network layer (TCP P2P gossip) provides the communication foundation. The data layer (DAG, mempool, ledger) manages transaction storage and state. The sortition layer (VRF lottery) selects a rotating committee of proposers. The consensus layer (weighted median) aggregates predictions into an emergent agreement. The reputation layer (dual-EMA + detection) identifies and penalizes adversarial nodes. The synchronization layer (cross-node batch gossip) ensures global ledger consistency.

The layered design enables each component to be optimized independently: the network layer can be replaced with libp2p without affecting consensus; the consensus median can be replaced with a different aggregation function without affecting reputation; the attack detectors can be extended without affecting transaction processing. This modularity, combined with the emergent consensus model, positions ANGP as a flexible and scalable foundation for decentralized applications.

Section 3

Elimination mechanics

Certificate decay + dual-EMA

cert(t) = max(0, 1 − (e(t) / T)γ)
T = 1.2
error scale at zero cert
γ = 4.27
decay steepness
RF(t) = αF·cert(t) + (1−αF)·RF(t−1)
RS(t) = αS·cert(t) + (1−αS)·RS(t−1)
R(t) = min(RF, RS) · HonestFloor

min (not arithmetic mean) ensures a single bad signal on either channel dominates — adversaries cannot average out a fast-channel attack by keeping the slow channel honest.

Three thresholds + cluster cap

R < 0.20

Single-seed per density

Each density run with one random seed. Per-density repeats (10 seeds) would tighten CIs by √10 ≈ 3.16. Current 95% CI for mean TPS is ±3.5%.

⏱

Patient-attack latency

1000–8000-step detection for Sleeper / Patient-Byz is the inherent cost of allowing new nodes a bootstrap grace period.

⚠

Configuration sensitivity

70% theoretical bound requires ρcl = 0.30 always enabled. Misconfig (ρcl = 1.0) reduces the bound to 33% traditional BFT level.

↓

Wilson CI independence

95% Wilson upper bound on true FPR is 1.94×10⁻⁸ (10K) / ≈1.1×10⁻⁸ (30K). Clopper-Pearson fallback (no independence) is ≈31% — truth lies between.

◎

Adaptive adversaries

T21 Intermittent-Coord and T22 Adaptive-ε-Evasion both detected and eliminated within 500–1500 steps at 10% density (5000-step run). No double-spend or theft observed.
